messages.content:
Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 35
  gender: Female
  ethnicity: Oceania
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Accountant
  trauma_type: Mugging or robbery
  pcl5: 71

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Triggers: Auditory (Footsteps): Footsteps behind or nearby, Offender Cues: Seeing the offender, Tactile (Unexpected Touch): Being touched unprepared
  Maladaptive Strategies: Self-Blame Rumination: I dwell on what I have done wrong, Dissociate Deliberately: deliberately try to leave my body or blank out, Rumination: Prevention: ruminate about how event could have been prevented
  Threat: Cannot Trust Safety: Even when others tell me I am safe I find it impossible to believe it, Threat in Delays: When something takes longer than expected I assume something bad is happening, Cannot Relax: I am unable to relax even when I know I am in a safe place
  Memory: Taste Vividness: I can taste what I tasted during the event when the memory returns, Bodily Reenactment: When memories come to mind of what happened, I feel my body is in the same position as when the frightening event occurred., Story Feels Unreal: The memory is so extreme it is hard to believe it actually happened to me
  Negative Appraisals: Character Blame: The event happened to me because of the sort of person I am, World is Dangerous: The world is a dangerous place, Self-Blame: The event happened because of the way I acted

Vignette:
Kealani traces the condensation on her water glass, her focus narrowed to the single bead of moisture rolling down its side. It is a small trick she has taught herself for moments like this, a way to deliberately blank out her mind when the familiar cascade begins. For the past eight months, since the evening she took a shortcut through the alley behind her office building, her life has been governed by these moments. The attack itself is a memory that feels both impossibly vivid and strangely unreal, like a scene from a movie she can’t believe she was in. She remembers the crisp autumn air, the sound of her own heels on the pavement, and then, another sound—the quick, heavy scrape of footsteps behind her. Before she could turn, a hand clamped down on her arm, spinning her around and slamming her back against the cold brick wall. In her memory, the rough texture of the brick is a physical sensation she can still feel, and when the images return unbidden, she often finds her body tensing into the same defensive posture, hands slightly raised as if to ward off a blow. The most persistent sensory fragment is the taste, an acrid, metallic tang of pure terror that flooded her mouth, a taste she can summon with perfect clarity and which often returns when she is startled.

At first, the primary struggle was the rumination. For weeks, she would lie awake next to her husband, Mark, replaying the event endlessly. She was certain that if she had just acted differently, it could have been prevented. If she hadn't stayed late to finish the quarterly reports, if she had just called a car, if she had screamed louder. This line of thinking soon curdled into a deeper conviction: the event happened because of the sort of person she is—too trusting, not aware enough. This belief settled into her bones, a harsh judgment that the world is a fundamentally dangerous place and she is uniquely ill-equipped to navigate it. She came to see the mugging not as a random act of violence, but as an indictment of her own character.

These beliefs now color every aspect of her life. At her accounting firm, the open-plan office has become a minefield. The sound of a colleague approaching her cubicle from behind sends a jolt of panic through her chest. A friendly tap on the shoulder from her manager once caused her to cry out, her body reacting as if to an assault. She felt her back flush against her chair, a phantom reenactment of being pinned to the wall. The danger feels even more acute outside. A few weeks ago, while walking to the subway, she froze mid-stride. Across the street, a man in a dark hooded sweatshirt stood leaning against a building, his build and posture uncannily similar to her attacker's. Her heart hammered against her ribs, and the metallic taste of fear flooded her mouth. Even after he turned and she saw it wasn't him, the terror lingered for hours. The encounter solidified a new certainty: he was still out there, and she could run into him at any moment. After that incident, she began arranging her work-from-home days to minimize time in the office, a decision that has subtly strained her relationship with her team.

Even at home, a place she knows should be safe, she cannot relax. Mark’s reassurances are meaningless; she finds it impossible to believe she is truly safe anywhere. If he is ten minutes late coming home from his construction job, her mind immediately constructs catastrophic scenarios. The delay isn't traffic; it’s proof that something terrible has happened, that the danger she now sees everywhere has finally caught up to him, too. The most painful consequence has been the growing distance between them. His attempts at casual affection, once a source of comfort, are now triggers. An unexpected touch around her waist as she does the dishes can make her flinch violently, the sensation inseparable from the memory of the attacker’s grip. She sees the hurt in his eyes but cannot explain the reaction in a way that makes sense, even to herself. It was after one such evening, when she recoiled from his embrace and retreated to the other side of the room, leaving him standing alone in the kitchen, that she knew she had to seek help. The world outside felt hostile and unpredictable, but now her internal world, and the sanctuary of her own home, was shrinking too. She is terrified that she will never feel safe in her own skin again, that the person she was before that night is gone for good.
